title_en: Wuxi Humei Thermal Power Engineering Co., Ltd. v. DBS Bank (Singapore) — dispute over letter of credit
ruling_gist_en: In a letter of credit dispute between the beneficiary and the issuing bank, it is a common defense that the issuing bank refuses to pay under the letter of credit on the ground that the documents submitted by the beneficiary contain discrepancies. A correct understanding and application of the 'strict compliance' standard for document examination, as established in the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits and the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Letter of Credit Dispute Cases, is crucial. Where the entry regarding the 'origin standard' on the certificate of origin is sufficient to fulfill the function of that document, the relevant data on the certificate can corroborate each other, and can also be cross-verified with the credit and the goods prices recorded in the commercial invoice (another document required by the credit), and there is no contradiction among the documents, it should be held that the discrepancy alleged by the issuing bank cannot be established. In a situation where the beneficiary's presentation is compliant, the issuing bank shall make payment.

full_text_en:
Wuxi Humei Thermal Power Engineering Co., Ltd. v.  
DBS Bank Ltd. — dispute over letter of credit  

【Ruling Summary】  

In a letter of credit dispute between a beneficiary and an issuing bank, it is a common defense for the issuing bank to refuse payment under the letter of credit on the ground that the documents presented by the beneficiary contain discrepancies. A correct understanding and application of the "strict compliance" document examination standard established in the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits and the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Letter of Credit Disputes requires that, where the entry on the certificate of origin regarding the "origin criterion" is sufficient to express the function of that document, the relevant data in the certificate can be mutually verified with each other, and can also be mutually verified with the price of the goods recorded in the commercial invoice, which is another document required by the letter of credit, and no inconsistency exists among the documents, the discrepancy claimed by the issuing bank shall be found not to be established. Where the beneficiary presents conforming documents, the issuing bank shall make payment.  

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court  

(2017) Supreme People's Court Final No. 327  

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): DBS Bank Ltd. (Singapore). Domicile: 3rd Floor, Tower 3, Marina Bay Financial Centre Commercial Building, 12 Marina Boulevard, Singapore.  
Representative: Su Weili, Executive Director of the bank.  
Agent ad litem: Jin Saibo, Beijing Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.  
Agent ad litem: Feng Jing, Beijing Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.  

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance): Wuxi Humei Thermal Power Engineering Co., Ltd. Domicile: 25/F, Building B, Runhua International Mansion, No. 1188 Taihu West Avenue, Wuxi City, Jiangsu Province, People's Republic of China.  
Legal Representative: Xia Rong, Executive Director of the company.  
Agent ad litem: Shan Shiwen, Jiangsu Taihu Law Firm.  
Agent ad litem: Qiao Yu, Jiangsu Taihu Law Firm.  

The appellant, DBS Bank Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as DBS Bank), appealed to this Court against the civil judgment (2014) Su Shang Wai Chu Zi No. 0004 rendered by the Jiangsu High People's Court in the case of a dispute over a letter of credit between it and the respondent, Wuxi Humei Thermal Power Engineering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Humei Company). This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing of this case on June 12, 2017. The agents ad litem of DBS Bank, Jin Saibo and Feng Jing, and the agents ad litem of Humei Company, Shan Shiwen and Qiao Yu, all appeared in court. The trial of this case has now been concluded.  

Humei Company alleged in its complaint: On June 10, 2013, DBS Bank, with Humei Company as the beneficiary, issued a letter of credit No. 553-01-1165349 for payment of the goods described therein. On November 29, 2013, Humei Company presented documents for payment to DBS Bank. On December 5, 2013, DBS Bank refused payment on the ground that the FOB price listed in Box 9 of the Certificate of Origin was the same as the CIF price shown on the invoice, constituting a discrepancy. The reason given by DBS Bank for refusing payment under the letter of credit was not valid. Therefore, Humei Company requested the court to order DBS Bank to pay the full amount under Letter of Credit No. 553-01-1165349, totaling USD 8,938,290.98, equivalent to RMB 55,448,732.79 (calculated at the exchange rate of 1:6.203505 as stipulated in the swap agreement between Humei Company and China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch), plus interest of RMB 1,321,654.7 from December 6, 2013, to May 1, 2014 (tentative) calculated at 6% per annum, the benchmark lending rate of the People's Bank of China for the same period.  

The court of first instance found: On June 10, 2013, DBS Bank, with Humei Company as the beneficiary, issued a sight payment letter of credit No. 553-01-1165349. Field 32B specified the total amount of the L/C as USD 8,938,290.98; Field 31D specified the expiry date of the L/C as December 5, 2013; Field 44C specified the latest shipment date as November 20, 2013; Field 46A, documents required, stipulated that upon presentation, Humei Company should submit, among others, a commercial invoice and a certificate of origin; Field 40E specified that the latest version of UCP would apply; Field 44E specified the port of loading as Shanghai, China; Field 44A, description of goods, specified: a set of power plant equipment for the PT DABI OLEO 2X90T/H+15MW power station under Contract HWM12-002, CIF Dumai, Indonesia.  

On October 8, 2013, and October 12, 2013, DBS Bank issued amendments to the L/C, modifying the latest shipment date and the expiry date of the L/C to November 30, 2013, and December 16, 2013, respectively.  

On November 29, 2013, Humei Company, through the advising bank, China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch, sent the full set of documents required by the L/C to DBS Bank via DHL courier. The commercial invoice showed the price terms of the transaction as CIF Dumai, Indonesia, valued at USD 8,938,290.98. The Certificate of Origin, in Box 7 (Number and kind of packages; description of goods, including corresponding quantity and HS code of the importer), contained, among other relevant content, "Power plant equipment for PT DABI OLEO 2X90T/H+15MW power station under Contract HWM12-002, CIF Dumai, Indonesia"; in Box 9 (Gross weight or other quantity and price (FOB)), contained, among other relevant content, "USD: 8,938,290.98".  

On December 5, 2013, DBS Bank, through the advising bank, China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch, issued a notice of refusal stating: "The FOB price listed in Box 9 of the Certificate of Origin is USD 8,938,290.98, while the invoice shows a CIF price of the same amount, i.e., USD 8,938,290.98, which constitutes a conflict. The aforementioned discrepancy is not acceptable to our bank, and we therefore refuse to pay the amount under the L/C."  

The court of first instance held that the issue in dispute was whether the discrepancy claimed by DBS Bank was established.  

(I) Regarding the applicable law for this case. DBS Bank is a legal person registered in Singapore, therefore the letter of credit relationship in this case constitutes a foreign-related civil relationship. Field 40E of the L/C explicitly stipulated that the "latest version of UCP" would apply, i.e., the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (International Chamber of Commerce Publication No. 600, hereinafter UCP600). Pursuant to Article 2 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Letter of Credit Disputes, the relevant provisions of UCP600 shall apply first to this case. Since the letter of credit relationship is a contractual relationship and the parties did not agree on the law applicable to matters not covered by UCP600 in the letter of credit relationship, pursuant to Article 41 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, the law of the place of habitual residence of the party whose performance of obligations best reflects the characteristics of the contract, or other law most closely connected with the contract, shall apply. In a letter of credit relationship, the beneficiary's obligation is to present conforming documents, and the issuing bank's obligation is to honour upon a determination that the presentation is complying. That is, the beneficiary will receive payment under the L/C as long as it presents conforming documents. Therefore, the beneficiary's performance of the obligation to deliver conforming documents best reflects the characteristics of the letter of credit relationship. Accordingly, for matters not covered by UCP600 in the letter of credit relationship in this case, the law of the place of domicile of Humei Company, i.e., the laws of the People's Republic of China, shall apply.  

(II) The discrepancy claimed by DBS Bank was not established, and DBS Bank shall pay Humei Company the amount under the L/C in question and bear corresponding liability for breach of contract.  

1. The discrepancy claimed by DBS Bank was not established. Article 14(f) of UCP600 provides: "If a credit requires presentation of a document other than a transport document, insurance document or commercial invoice, without stipulating the issuer of the document or its data content, banks will accept the document as presented if its content appears to fulfil the function of the required document and otherwise complies with sub-article 14(d)." Article 14(d) of UCP600 provides: "Data in a document, when read in context with the credit, the document itself and international standard banking practice, need not be identical to, but must not conflict with, data in that document, any other stipulated document or the credit." The Certificate of Origin at issue in this case is a document other than a transport document, insurance document or commercial invoice required by the credit, and the credit did not stipulate the issuer or data content of the Certificate of Origin. Accordingly, banks must accept this Certificate of Origin provided it meets the following two conditions: (1) the content of the Certificate of Origin appears to fulfil the function of a certificate of origin under the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area; and (2) it otherwise complies with the provisions of sub-article 14(d). The transaction in this case is a CIF transaction. The invoice number and date, description of goods, contract number, and CIF price recorded in the Certificate of Origin were consistent with the content of the invoice, and the declarant's declaration box in the Certificate of Origin explicitly stated that "It is hereby certified, on the basis of the control carried out, that the declaration by the exporter is correct." Obviously, this Certificate of Origin could be appropriately linked to the goods in question and was signed by an authorized signatory. The content of the Certificate of Origin appeared to fulfil the function of a certificate of origin under the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area. DBS Bank did not dispute this. The discrepancy on which DBS Bank relied to refuse payment was that the FOB price listed in Box 9 of the Certificate of Origin and the CIF price shown on the commercial invoice were the same, both USD 8,938,290.98, constituting a conflict in violation of Article 14(d) of UCP600. The court of first instance held that this discrepancy claimed by DBS Bank could not be established. The reasons are as follows: First, DBS Bank's comparison of different types of data violated the document examination rule under Article 14(d) of UCP600, which requires the comparison of the same type of data. The requirement of "identical to" in Article 14(d) of UCP600 means that when examining documents, banks must compare data that are of the same type; otherwise, it would be impossible to be "identical to". "Need not be identical to" does not mean that banks are authorized to compare data of different types. Rather, it requires that when comparing data of the same type, banks should not be overly mechanical as to apply a "mirror image" standard; minor differences between data of the same type are permitted, provided those minor differences do not lead to conflict or ambiguity. This still reflects the document examination rule of comparing data of the same type. International Standard Banking Practice (hereinafter ISBP745), the ICC Banking Commission, and the judicial practice of the People's Republic of China all hold this view. ISBP745 paragraph A22 provides: "A misspelling or typing error that does not affect the meaning of the word or the sentence in which it occurs does not constitute a document discrepancy. For example, a description of goods as 'mashine' instead of 'machine', 'fountan pen' instead of 'fountain pen', or 'modle' instead of 'model' would not be regarded as conflicting data under sub-article 14(d) of UCP600. However, a description as 'model 321' instead of 'model 123' would be regarded as conflicting data under that sub-article." The official opinion of the ICC Banking Commission, R740 (Consultation TA 722rev), held that a difference between the contract number on another document and that on the invoice constituted conflicting data under Article 14(d) of UCP600. In the civil ruling (2010) Min Shen Zi No. 112 of the Supreme People's Court of the People's Republic of China in the case of Korea Exchange Bank v. Bank of Qingdao Co., Ltd., it was held that a discrepancy between the letter of credit number indicated in the "Non-Wooden Packaging Material Declaration" and the number of the letter of credit in question constituted conflicting data under Article 14(d) of UCP600. In the above examples, the data being compared were all of the same type, such as "description of goods," "contract number," "letter of credit number," etc. It can be seen that banks, when examining documents, must follow the rule of comparing data of the same type. This is not only an inherent requirement of UCP600 but also a consistent requirement of international standard banking practice, the ICC Banking Commission, and judicial precedents. Therefore, in this case, when examining the price of the goods, DBS Bank should have examined whether there was a conflict between the CIF price in the credit and the documents, and among the documents themselves, because the CIF price of the goods appeared in the L/C, the commercial invoice, and the Certificate of Origin. It should not have compared the CIF price of the goods with the FOB price. DBS Bank compared the CIF price with the FOB price, which clearly violated the document examination rule under Article 14(d) of UCP600 that requires comparison of data of the same type. Second, DBS Bank had no authority to examine the appropriateness of the FOB price of the goods. The appearance of the FOB price of the goods in Box 9 of the Certificate of Origin is a requirement of the Certificate of Origin itself. The examination of whether the FOB price of the goods is appropriate is the function of the customs authorities of the destination country. Except for the Certificate of Origin, the FOB price of the goods did not appear in the L/C or other documents, nor could it appear. This shows that neither the applicant nor the beneficiary of the L/C intended to authorize DBS Bank to examine the FOB price of the goods when examining documents. Therefore, there is no basis for examining whether the FOB price in the credit and the documents, or among the documents themselves, is consistent or conflicting. DBS Bank had no authority to examine the FOB price of the goods. DBS Bank, by arbitrarily comparing the FOB price of the goods with the CIF price and refusing to pay under the L/C on the ground that the FOB price being the same as the CIF price constituted a discrepancy, was in effect examining the appropriateness of the FOB price, which constitutes an intervention in the underlying transaction. This practice of DBS Bank violated the fundamental principle of UCP600 that banks, when examining documents, must not intervene in the underlying transaction. In conclusion, the discrepancy raised by DBS Bank based on a comparison of two different types of data, the CIF price and the FOB price of the goods, did not comply with the provisions of Article 14(d) of UCP600 and was invalid.  

2. DBS Bank shall pay the amount under the L/C in question and compensate for the corresponding losses. Since the discrepancy on which DBS Bank relied to refuse payment is not established, DBS Bank shall pay Humei Company the amount of USD 8,938,290.98 under the L/C in question. Regarding the method of performance, Humei Company claimed that the above USD amount be converted at the exchange rate of 1:6.203505 as stipulated in the swap agreement between Humei Company and China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch, requesting the court to order DBS Bank to pay the equivalent of RMB 55,448,732.79. DBS Bank did not object. The court of first instance upheld Humei Company's request. Therefore, the amount to be paid by DBS Bank is RMB 55,448,732.79. Pursuant to Article 14(b) of UCP600, an issuing bank shall determine, within a maximum of five banking days following the day of presentation, whether the presentation is complying. On November 29, 2013, Humei Company, through the advising bank, China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch, sent the full set of documents required by the L/C to DBS Bank via DHL courier. On December 5, 2013, DBS Bank, through the advising bank, China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch, issued the notice of refusal. This shows that DBS Bank completed its document examination no later than December 5, 2013, which complied with the above provision. Since the L/C in question is a sight payment credit, pursuant to Article 15(a) of UCP600, when a presentation is complying, the bank must honour at sight. Therefore, the time for DBS Bank to perform its payment obligation was at the latest December 5, 2013. DBS Bank's improper refusal to pay constituted a breach of contract and shall bear corresponding liability for breach of contract. Since the parties did not agree on the method of liability for breach of contract, the liability of DBS Bank shall be determined in accordance with statutory methods. Humei Company claimed that DBS Bank should pay compensation for losses due to overdue payment from December 6, 2013, until the date of actual payment, calculated at the benchmark lending rate for RMB loans of the People's Bank of China for the same period. This claim is consistent with the relevant provisions of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and is upheld.  

In conclusion, the discrepancy claimed by DBS Bank was not established, and DBS Bank shall pay the amount under the L/C in question to Humei Company and compensate for the losses caused to Humei Company by its overdue payment. In accordance with Article 14(a), (b), (d), (f), Article 15(a) of UCP600, Article 174 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 24(4) and Article 45(2) of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Disputes over Sales Contracts, and Article 142 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of first instance adjudicated as follows: 1. DBS Bank shall pay Humei Company RMB 55,448,732.79 within ten days after the judgment takes effect; 2. DBS Bank shall pay Humei Company compensation for losses due to overdue payment on the above amount from December 6, 2013, until the date of actual payment, calculated at the benchmark lending rate for RMB loans of the People's Bank of China for the same period within ten days after the judgment takes effect. If DBS Bank fails to perform its monetary payment obligation within the period specified in the judgment, it shall pay double the interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance in accordance with Article 253 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The court acceptance fee of RMB 325,652 shall be borne by DBS Bank.

DBS Bank, dissatisfied with the foregoing judgment of first instance, appealed to this Court, alleging: (1) The judgment of first instance omitted important facts. On December 24, 2013, Humei Company sent DBS Bank an "Objection to the Refusal Notice under Letter of Credit No. 553-01-1165349," in which it acknowledged that the FOB price entered in the certificate of origin was actually the CIF price, with the intention of making the amount of that FOB price exactly equal to the CIF price on the insurance policy and invoice, so as to ensure compliance of the documents. This fact proves that Humei Company, based on a mistaken understanding of the principle of documentary compliance under UCP600, actively created a discrepancy in the documents. (2) The judgment of first instance erred in restricting the issuing bank's core right to examine documents and their content based on the terms of the letter of credit it issued. Pursuant to UCP600 Article 14, paragraphs a, d, and f, the issuing bank determines, based solely on the documents themselves, whether they appear on their face to constitute a complying presentation. Data in a document must not conflict with data in that document, any other required document, or the credit. The letter of credit in this case clearly stipulated the documents to be presented by the beneficiary in clause 46A. The certificate of origin was a primary document required by the credit. Its main function, in addition to certifying the origin of the goods, was to show and confirm the basis for determining the origin of the goods and/or services and the calculation basis for customs clearance and taxation by displaying the detailed FOB price of the goods. The issuing bank was entitled to examine all required documents and their content in accordance with the CIF price terms described in clause 45A of the credit, and also had the right to examine the documents and their content based on the amount in clause 32B and whether it fell within the allowed tolerance range in clause 39A. The issuing bank was entitled to examine the content of box 9 of the certificate of origin, because the goods description and value stated in that box were closely related to the amount the beneficiary could draw under the credit and the permitted percentage tolerance of the credit amount. The FOB price of the goods shown in box 9 of the certificate of origin only included the price of the goods when they passed the ship's rail at the Chinese port of loading, whereas the CIF price required by the credit and shown in the commercial invoice and insurance policy was the price of the goods delivered to the port of destination. The figures behind these two prices were exactly the same, both USD 8,938,290.98, which clearly constituted a contradiction in data between documents. This is a matter of commercial common sense. This case does not involve a typographical error in the documents. The issuing bank only conducted a surface examination of the documents and their content based on the requirements of clauses 45A, 32B, and 39A of the credit, concluded that the documents were discrepant, and then refused payment. It did not examine the appropriateness of the FOB price under the underlying contract. The court of first instance's view that document examination only allows comparing "data of the same kind" and not comparing data of different kinds is erroneous. In this case, the FOB price in the certificate of origin was not content the credit required the beneficiary to provide; it was content voluntarily submitted by the beneficiary, and it certainly fell within the scope of the issuing bank's examination. The issuing bank's finding that this constituted a discrepancy based on a commercially unreasonable inconsistency in the goods value information in the document was not improper. (3) The judgment of first instance ordering DBS Bank to pay the principal amount of the letter of credit converted into RMB and interest calculated at the RMB loan rate lacks legal basis. The letter of credit transaction in this case was an international transaction denominated in USD. Humei Company claimed the amount payable under the letter of credit, so it should be calculated in USD. Furthermore, interest on the principal of the letter of credit should be calculated using the prevailing USD base interest rate in international financial markets, namely the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR). According to the published LIBOR, the annual interest rate for USD on the due date claimed by Humei Company, December 6, 2013, was 0.57670%. In summary, the judgment of first instance had unclear findings of fact and erroneous application of law. It requested the revocation of the judgment of first instance and the amendment to dismiss all of Humei Company's claims.

Humei Company replied: (1) The court of first instance's findings of fact were accurate, and its reasoning that DBS Bank's grounds for refusal were untenable was clear, comprehensive, and well-founded. The certificate of origin involved in this case was a document other than the transport document, insurance document, or commercial invoice required by the credit, and the credit did not stipulate the issuer or data content of the certificate of origin. The court of first instance correctly held that, as long as the certificate of origin met two conditions — first, the content of the certificate of origin appeared to satisfy the function of a preferential tariff certificate of origin under the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area, and second, it otherwise complied with UCP600 Article 14(d) — the bank must accept it. This was entirely consistent with UCP600 Article 14(f) and also consistent with ISBP745. The transaction involved was a CIF transaction. The invoice number, date, goods name, contract number, and CIF price recorded in the certificate of origin were consistent with the content of the invoice, and the declarant's statement box in the certificate of origin clearly indicated that "Based on the controls carried out, it is hereby certified that the declaration by the exporter is correct." Obviously, the certificate of origin appeared to satisfy the function of a preferential tariff certificate of origin under the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area. Box 8 of the certificate of origin was filled with "WO" (wholly obtained), indicating that the goods were 100% produced in the exporting country, so whatever number was entered in box 9 would not affect the tariff treatment enjoyed by the importer. The goods described in the certificate of origin in this case were the same goods as those described in the commercial invoice. The requirement of "equivalent consistency" under UCP600 Article 14(d) requires the bank, when examining documents, to compare data of the same kind; otherwise, "equivalent consistency" is impossible. Except for the appearance of FOB in box 9 of the certificate of origin, FOB did not appear in the credit or in the documents required by the credit, such as the bill of lading, invoice, or insurance policy. DBS Bank had no basis or prerequisite for comparison. Examining the FOB value, when it was not required by the credit or by other documents stipulated in the credit, and comparing it with the CIF price data in the invoice, and then inferring a contradiction between the FOB value and the CIF price because the figures were the same, constituted interference with the underlying transaction and violated the fundamental principles of UCP600. Before filing this lawsuit, Humei Company obtained Decision No. 331 of the International Chamber of Commerce International Centre for Expertise (DOCDEX) on the dispute involved. Its conclusion was that DBS Bank's objection was invalid and DBS Bank must pay the amount under the letter of credit to Humei Company. It considered that the trade term CIF Dumai, Indonesia in the certificate of origin was consistent with the credit; the term "FOB" in box 9 of the certificate of origin did not indicate any trade term other than CIF Dumai, Indonesia for this transaction; the data in box 9 (FOB) of the certificate of origin was not required by the credit or UCP600; DBS Bank's objection was invalid because it arose from a comparison of two different types of data, namely the value under the trade term CIF Dumai, Indonesia compared with the gross weight or other quantity and FOB value, rather than a comparison with the trade term FOB followed by the name of the port of loading; in the absence of a requirement in the credit, whether these values were different or the same was irrelevant. Furthermore, the certificate of origin involved in this case was a standard format established by international treaties and agreements between China and ASEAN countries. The treaties and agreements between China and ASEAN countries do not prohibit the parties to a transaction from using other trade terms, nor do they stipulate that the parties can only use the FOB trade term. Therefore, inferring that "(FOB)" in box 9 of the certificate of origin in this case was a trade term was erroneous. According to UCP600 Article 14(g), a bank may disregard or return documents not required by the credit. Accordingly, when not required by the credit, DBS Bank had no right to examine "(FOB)." The discrepancy raised by DBS Bank did not comply with UCP600 Article 14(a) and (d). The certificate of origin and other documents provided by Humei Company satisfied the requirements of UCP600 Article 14(f), and DBS Bank must honor the payment under the letter of credit. (2) Regarding the issue of paying the amount under the letter of credit in USD, Humei Company agreed with DBS Bank's opinion that the judgment should be amended to order DBS Bank to pay the amount under the letter of credit in USD; however, LIBOR was not the interest rate agreed upon by the parties; the interest rate stipulated by Chinese law should apply. The judgment of first instance ordering DBS Bank to pay interest to Humei Company complied with the provisions of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Disputes over Sales Contracts, but the calculation of interest payable by DBS Bank without applying the overdue penalty interest rate standard stipulated in the aforementioned provisions was inappropriate. Interest payable by DBS Bank to Humei Company should be calculated based on RMB 55,448,732.79 and the overdue payment penalty interest rate. In summary, it requested the dismissal of DBS Bank's appeal, an amendment to order DBS Bank to pay the amount under the letter of credit in USD, and calculation of the interest payable by DBS Bank to Humei Company based on RMB 55,448,732.79 and the overdue payment penalty interest rate.

During the second instance of this Court, neither party submitted new evidence. DBS Bank argued that the judgment of first instance omitted certain facts that were not in dispute between the parties during the first instance proceedings, namely: On December 24, 2013, Humei Company sent DBS Bank an "Objection to the Refusal Notice under Letter of Credit No. 553-01-1165349," in which it stated: "The certificate of origin issued by Jiangsu Entry-Exit Inspection and Quarantine Bureau required by the credit can satisfy the function of a certificate of origin, i.e., to certify origin, and the price entered in box 9 of the certificate of origin is exactly the same as the prices in the commercial invoice and insurance policy. Even if box 9 of the certificate of origin requires the FOB price and, to ensure that the amounts shown in the insurance policy, invoice, and certificate of origin are exactly the same, the CIF price was entered into the certificate of origin, treating this exactly same data as a discrepancy violates UCP600 Article 14(d) and (f)." Humei Company had no objection to this. This Court confirms this fact.

Opinion of the Court: This case arises from a dispute over payment under a letter of credit between the issuing bank and the beneficiary. The court of first instance correctly applied UCP600 and the relevant provisions of Chinese law in hearing this case, and the parties have no objection to this.

The focus of the dispute in this case is whether there were discrepancies in the documents presented under the letter of credit involved.

(1) On the issue of whether there were discrepancies in the documents presented under the letter of credit involved

According to the documentary requirements of the letter of credit involved, the beneficiary Humei Company was required to present "one original certificate of origin and three copies." UCP600 Article 14 sets out the standards for examining documents. Paragraph f states: "If a credit requires presentation of a document other than a transport document, insurance document or commercial invoice, without stipulating the issuer of the document or its data content, banks will accept the document as presented if its content appears to fulfill the function of the required document and otherwise complies with sub-article 14(d)." UCP600 Article 14(d) states: "Data in a document, when read in context with the credit, the document itself and international standard banking practice, need not be identical to, but must not conflict with, data in that document, any other stipulated document or the credit." According to the above provisions, although UCP600 establishes a strict compliance standard of "on their face," it does not require absolute exactness. As long as the documents do not conflict with the requirements of the credit and with each other, the presentation should be deemed compliant, and the issuing bank must pay. Article 6, paragraph 1 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Letter of Credit Disputes stipulates: "When a people's court tries a letter of credit dispute case involving the examination of documents, it shall, according to the relevant international practices or other provisions agreed upon by the parties, determine whether the documents on their face comply with the terms of the credit and whether the documents are consistent with each other; if the parties have not agreed, the court shall determine compliance in accordance with the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits of the International Chamber of Commerce and the relevant standards established by the International Chamber of Commerce." Paragraph 2 stipulates: "If documents under a letter of credit are not completely identical on their face with the terms of the credit or with each other, but do not cause ambiguity, it shall not be deemed a discrepancy." This provision is consistent with the spirit of UCP600 Article 14 regarding document examination standards.

In this case, the beneficiary Humei Company presented a certificate of origin to the issuing bank DBS Bank. The certificate of origin was a standard form titled "Certificate of Origin under Preferential Tariff of China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (Declaration and Certificate Combined) Form E." In box 7, "Number and kind of packages; description of goods (including quantity and HS code of importer)," the following information was entered: "A set of power plant equipment under Contract HWM12-002 for PT DABI OLEO 2X90T/H+ 15MW Power Plant, CIF Dumai, Indonesia." In box 8, "Origin criterion," "WO" (wholly obtained in the exporting country) was entered. In box 9, "Gross weight or other quantity and price (FOB)," "USD: 8938290.98" was entered. In box 12, "Certification," the issuer signed: "Based on the controls carried out, it is hereby certified that the declaration by the exporter is correct." According to UCP600 Article 14(f) and (d), as long as the content of this certificate of origin appears to fulfill its function, and the data in it does not conflict with the data required by the credit or the data in other documents required by the credit, the presentation should be deemed compliant.

Since the certificate of origin is a standard form, the parties cannot modify the names of its boxes. The "(FOB)" in box 9 is part of the standard box name. This expression "(FOB)" should not be understood as the FOB price of goods under international trade terms, for the following reasons: First, this expression does not conform to the basic format of international trade terms. International trade terms primarily describe the allocation of obligations, costs, and risks involved in the transportation of goods from seller to buyer. According to the Incoterms 2010, effective January 1, 2011, FOB is an abbreviation for "Free on Board (named port of shipment)," meaning "the seller delivers the goods on board the vessel nominated by the buyer at the named port of shipment or procures the goods already so delivered. The risk of loss of or damage to the goods passes when the goods are on board the vessel, and the buyer bears all costs from that moment onwards." CIF is an abbreviation for "Cost, Insurance and Freight (named port of destination)," meaning "the seller delivers the goods on board the vessel or procures the goods already so delivered. The risk of loss of or damage to the goods passes when the goods are on board the vessel. The seller must contract for and pay the costs and freight necessary to bring the goods to the named port of destination." In this case, the expression "(FOB)" lacks the "(named port of shipment)" component, which clearly does not conform to the format requirements of international trade terms. Second, as can be seen from the Incoterms 2010, the FOB price and CIF price under international trade terms have significantly different components and cannot simply be converted using a formula or other means. The certificate of origin standard form serves international trade within the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area. International trade within the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area cannot possibly allow parties to use only the FOB price to the exclusion of other prices. If "(FOB)" in box 9 of the form were understood as the FOB price of goods under international trade terms, it would clearly not meet market demands. In summary, understanding "(FOB)" in box 9 of the certificate of origin form as the FOB price under international trade terms is not reasonable. A reasonable understanding of this "(FOB)" is that it is indicative, guiding the party to enter the corresponding price of the goods in this box.

The price of the goods under the underlying contract was "CIF Dumai, Indonesia." The amount of the letter of credit was USD 8,938,290.98. To comply with the credit requirements, the beneficiary Humei Company entered USD 8,938,290.98 directly in box 9 of the certificate of origin. Box 7 of the certificate of origin already contained information such as "A set of power plant equipment under Contract HWM12-002 for PT DABI OLEO 2X90T/H+ 15MW Power Plant, CIF Dumai, Indonesia," and together with "USD: 8938290.98" entered in box 9, these were mutually corroborative and could also corroborate the goods price recorded in the credit and the other document required by the credit, the commercial invoice. More importantly, box 8, "Origin criterion," was filled with "WO" (wholly obtained in the exporting country), which sufficiently expressed the function of the document. That is to say, although the data in box 9 of the certificate of origin was consistent with the CIF price data required by the credit and its documents, there was no contradiction between the documents, and no ambiguity would arise from understanding the document. Therefore, it should not be deemed a discrepancy.

Accordingly, the discrepancy claimed by the issuing bank DBS Bank cannot be established. When the beneficiary Humei Company made a complying presentation, DBS Bank should pay Humei Company. DBS Bank's grounds of appeal that the judgment of first instance erred in its determination of the discrepancy and that it had the right to refuse payment under the letter of credit cannot be sustained.

(2) On the issue of the currency for payment and the standard for calculating interest under the letter of credit in this case

The price of the goods under this letter of credit was calculated in USD. However, Humei Company, as the plaintiff in this case, made the following claim in its complaint: requesting a judgment that DBS Bank pay the full amount under Letter of Credit No. 553-01-1165349, totaling USD 8,938,290.98, converted to RMB 55,448,732.79 (calculated at the exchange rate of 1:6.203505 agreed in the currency swap contract between Humei Company and China Construction Bank Wuxi Branch) plus interest of RMB 1,321,654.7 calculated from December 6, 2013 to May 1, 2014 (tentative) at the benchmark loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China of 6% per annum. It can be seen that the judgment of first instance, in its ruling, calculated the principal in RMB and calculated interest based on the benchmark loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the corresponding period, which was consistent with the parties' claims and was not inappropriate. DBS Bank's ground of appeal that the judgment of first instance lacked legal basis for calculating the payment amount under the letter of credit in RMB and calculating interest at the RMB loan rate cannot be sustained. Humei Company, as the plaintiff, could not change its claims after the conclusion of the first instance court debate, nor did it file an appeal. Therefore, its defense in the second instance requesting a change in the judgment regarding the currency of the principal and the standard for calculating interest cannot be supported.

In summary, DBS Bank's appeal lacks merit and shall be dismissed. The first-instance judgment, except for omission of certain facts, correctly found the basic facts and correctly applied the law, and shall be affirmed. Pursuant to Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this court hereby orders as follows:

Appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.

The court acceptance fee for the second instance of RMB 325,652 shall be borne by DBS Bank Ltd., Singapore.

This judgment is final.
